title: Boeing soars 29% as the Afghanistan invasion sends money into defence stocks
what: Boeing shares rose 29% in January, far ahead of a market up 6%. Soviet troops entered Afghanistan on 25 December, and with American diplomats still held hostage in Tehran, President Carter told Congress on 23 January that any attempt by an outside power to seize the Persian Gulf would be repelled by force, and asked for military spending to rise 5% a year above inflation for five years. Investors turned to the arms makers: Boeing builds the B-52 bombers and Minuteman missiles the Air Force relies on, and its air-launched cruise missile is in a fly-off against a rival design.
why: The one unexplained big month of the Boeing arc, now hung on the Carter Doctrine and the defence rally. The context (invasion date, the 23 January speech, the 5% pledge, the cruise-missile competition decided in March 1980) is sourced; that Boeing rose because of it is inferred from the timing and the sector move, not stated by a source read. Curator asked for this story.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Doctrine (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AGM-86_ALCM (read 2026-10-03); monthly price change from data/out/ba.json

title: The 767 flies as airlines suffer
what: The Boeing 767 made its first flight on 26 September. When it was rolled out in August, Boeing had 173 firm orders from 17 customers. It is designed to burn 20 to 30% less fuel than older jets and to need only two pilots, which a presidential task force accepted as safe in July.
why: The product cycle that carries Boeing through the decade. The stock nonetheless halved in 1981 (-49%), the worst calendar year in its history, as high interest rates and recession hit airlines; no single Boeing event was found for that fall.

title: Wall Street jumps on rate hopes; Boeing up 48%, Apple up 33%
what: After the Dow hit a low of 777 on 12 August, it jumped a record 39 points on the 17th, when an influential Salomon Brothers economist said interest rates would fall, and trading topped 100 million shares a day for the first time. The Federal Reserve has let interest rates come down: the rate banks charge each other averaged about 10 percent in August, against 14 percent in June, as unemployment reached 9.8 percent and inflation slowed to 6.4 percent (July). The shares that had fallen furthest rose most: Boeing gained 48% in August and Apple Computer 33%. On 19 August Boeing delivered its first 767 to United Airlines. The numbers: the Fed's rate 10.1 percent. Inflation 6.6 percent. Unemployment 9.8 percent.
why: Explains the +48% month, Boeing's best: a deeply cyclical stock rebounding from the 1981 crash as rates fall (market +12%). Review 2026-10: title "Wall Street's great rally starts" named the bull market before it was one. [Curator note applied 2026-10-04: "Add a note about Apple. Don't foreshadow the "great rally"."]
source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1982/08/18/Wall-Street-has-first-100-million-share-day/9743398491200/ (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_767 (read 2026-10-03). title: The Boeing 767 carries its first passengers
what: Boeing delivered the first 767 to United Airlines on 19 August, and on 8 September it flew its first paying passengers from Chicago to Denver. The 767 is Boeing's first wide-body aircraft with only two engines, and the first big jet flown by two pilots instead of three, helped by computer screens in the cockpit. It seats about 216 people. Boeing spent 3.5 to 4 billion dollars developing it together with its smaller sister, the 757; United ordered the first 30 back in 1978.
why: Two engines and two pilots make flying cheaper: the 767 opens the age of twin-engine jets across the oceans and sells for more than forty years.
changed: new beat from a note to the writer (the note sat on an Apple beat)

title: Machinists strike as Boeing struggles to build enough planes
what: Boeing's machinists went on strike on 5 October, demanding higher pay and less mandatory overtime. Many have been working seven-day weeks and up to 200 hours of forced overtime every three months as Boeing tries to keep up with orders; airlines ordered 322 757s alone in 1988 and 1989.
why: A boom problem: too many orders. The strike ended after 48 days on 22 November and cost about 2.5 billion dollars of revenue; the stock still rose 47% in 1989.

title: Boeing launches the 737 Next Generation
what: On 17 November Boeing announced the 737 Next Generation, an updated family of its best-selling small jet, with new wings and engines, to compete with the Airbus A320.
why: The workhorse that funded Boeing for the next twenty years and the base on which the 737 MAX was later built.

title: The 777 enters service
what: United Airlines put the Boeing 777 into passenger service in June. It is the first airliner designed entirely on computers and the first approved for long flights over water on two engines from the day it entered service.
why: The start of a strong run: the stock rose 67% in 1995 and 36% in 1996.

title: Asia's crisis forces Boeing to cut production
what: On 1 December Boeing said it will cut production of the 747 from 3.5 to 2 planes a month in late 1999, and possibly to 1, and slow the 757, 767 and 777 too. 'The economic slowdown in Asia is driving air traffic down,' said Alan Mulally, head of commercial airplanes.
why: Explains the -20% month; Boeing's low point of the 1990s.

title: Chief executive Phil Condit resigns over the tanker scandal
what: On 1 December Boeing said chief executive Phil Condit has resigned; Harry Stonecipher, the former McDonnell Douglas chief, takes over. Boeing had fired its finance chief over the hiring of an Air Force procurement official who had worked on a deal to lease Boeing tankers, and the Pentagon has frozen the deal. Airbus is overtaking Boeing as the leading airliner maker this year.
why: The low point of Boeing's reputation in the 2000s; the stock bottomed in early 2003.

title: Boeing launches the 7E7 Dreamliner
what: On 26 April Boeing's board approved the 7E7 Dreamliner, a new mid-size long-range jet made largely of carbon composites, after All Nippon Airways ordered 50, worth about 6 billion dollars. It is the largest launch order for a new Boeing jet, with first deliveries planned for 2008.
why: The plane that later became the 787: a huge seller, three years late and plagued by problems, but the backbone of the 2005-2007 and 2013-2018 rallies.

title: Jim McNerney becomes chief executive
what: Boeing's board named Jim McNerney, head of 3M and a former GE executive, as chairman and chief executive on 30 June. His predecessor Harry Stonecipher was forced out in March over a relationship with a female executive.
why: A decade of McNerney: big 787 and 737 MAX decisions and large share buybacks.

title: The 787 Dreamliner is unveiled
what: Boeing showed its first 787 Dreamliner to about 15,000 people in Everett on 8 July, broadcast to 45 countries. It is the fastest-selling new jet in Boeing's history.
why: The peak of the 2000s boom: the stock's July 2007 high was not passed until 2013. In October Boeing delayed first deliveries by six months, the first of many delays.

title: The 787 finally flies
what: The Boeing 787 Dreamliner completed its first flight on 15 December, more than two years late. In June Boeing had postponed it again to reinforce a part of the wing-body joint, and in August it set a new schedule and took a charge.
why: The end of the worst of the 787 saga; first delivery followed in September 2011.

title: First 787 delivered to ANA
what: Boeing handed over the first 787 Dreamliner to All Nippon Airways on 25-26 September, three years later than the 2008 date planned at launch.
why: The 787 starts earning. In 2011, pushed by the Airbus A320neo, Boeing also chose to re-engine the 737 (the MAX) instead of designing a new plane.

title: Battery fires ground the 787
what: After a battery fire on an empty Japan Airlines 787 in Boston on 7 January and a battery problem on an ANA flight, the US Federal Aviation Administration grounded the whole 787 fleet on 16 January, the first grounding of an airliner type since the DC-10 in 1979.
why: A scare that passed: flights resumed in April with redesigned batteries, and the stock rose 81% in 2013.

title: Dennis Muilenburg to succeed McNerney
what: On 23 June Boeing named its chief operating officer, Dennis Muilenburg, as chief executive from 1 July, succeeding Jim McNerney. Muilenburg, an engineer, joined Boeing as an intern.
why: The CEO of the buyback boom and of the 737 MAX crashes.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Boeing (read 2026-10-03, citing Boeing release 2015-06-23 and Business Insider 2015-06-23); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Muilenburg (read 2026-10-03)

title: Boeing guides to fewer deliveries
what: On 27 January Boeing reported record 2015 revenue of 96.1 billion dollars and 762 deliveries, but forecast 740 to 745 deliveries in 2016 and lower fourth-quarter airliner profits after a charge on the 747.
why: Explains the -17% month (market -5%): the first sign the airliner boom might plateau. It did not: 2017 was +89%.

title: Cash floods in: Boeing raises its forecast
what: On 26 July Boeing reported strong second-quarter results, operating cash flow of 5 billion dollars and 2.5 billion dollars of share buybacks in the quarter, and raised its earnings and cash flow forecasts.
why: Explains the +23% month. The cash machine phase: Boeing returned most of its cash to shareholders and the stock nearly doubled in 2017, peaking in February 2019.

title: A new 737 MAX crashes in Indonesia
what: On 29 October a Lion Air Boeing 737 MAX 8 crashed after take-off from Jakarta, killing all 189 people on board. The MAX is the newest version of Boeing's best-selling jet and has been in service for little more than a year.
why: The first of the two MAX crashes; Boeing began redesigning the MCAS flight control software right after it, but the plane kept flying.

title: Second crash: the 737 MAX is grounded worldwide
what: On 10 March an Ethiopian Airlines 737 MAX 8 crashed after take-off from Addis Ababa, killing all 157 on board, in circumstances similar to the Lion Air crash. China grounded the plane the next day, others followed, and on 13 March the US FAA became the last major regulator to ground it. Boeing's shares had their biggest fall since 2001.
why: The defining crisis. The MAX, Boeing's best-selling plane, stayed grounded for 20 months; the February 2019 price was the all-time high.

title: Boeing halts MAX production and fires its CEO
what: On 16 December Boeing said it will suspend 737 MAX production in January, as the plane's return to service drags on. On 23 December the board dismissed chief executive Dennis Muilenburg and named chairman Dave Calhoun to replace him.
why: The MAX crisis reaches the top; a $4.9 billion charge for airline compensation had been booked in July.
source: https://boeing.mediaroom.com/2019-12-16-Boeing-Statement-Regarding-737-MAX-Production (title seen in release list, 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_737_MAX_groundings (read 2026-10-03, citing Reuters 2019-12-23); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Boeing (read 2026-10-03, July 2019 charge)

title: Pandemic on top of the MAX: Boeing suspends its dividend
what: With air travel collapsing because of Covid-19 and the MAX still grounded, Boeing on 20 March suspended its dividend and extended its halt on buybacks; chief executive Dave Calhoun gives up his pay for the year. On 23 March it said it will stop production in the Seattle area for 14 days.
why: Explains the -46% month, Boeing's worst in the game: a company already bleeding cash from the MAX loses its customers' business overnight.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/12927/000001292720000030/exhibit991.htm (Boeing release of 2020-03-20, read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/12927/000001292720000033/exhibit991.htm (Boeing release of 2020-03-23, read 2026-10-03)

title: Test flights for the MAX's return
what: From 28 June the FAA began three days of certification flight tests of the modified 737 MAX, a key step toward letting it fly again. Stock markets have recovered much of their spring losses as economies reopen.
why: Explains the +26% month: hope for the MAX and for travel. In May Boeing had announced more than 12,000 job cuts.

title: A vaccine, and the MAX is cleared to fly
what: On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech said their Covid-19 vaccine was more than 90% effective, and travel stocks soared. On 18 November the FAA ended the 737 MAX's 20-month grounding, the longest ever for a US airliner, subject to fixes on each plane and new pilot training.
why: Explains the +46% month, Boeing's second best in the game.

title: Boeing pays 2.5 billion dollars to settle MAX fraud charge
what: On 7 January Boeing agreed to pay more than 2.5 billion dollars to settle a US criminal charge that it hid information from safety regulators about the MAX: a 243.6 million dollar penalty, 1.77 billion dollars for airline customers and a 500 million dollar fund for crash victims' families.
why: Closes the legal chapter, or seemed to; the agreement came back to haunt Boeing after the 2024 door-plug blowout.

title: Another quarterly loss and the 777X slips to 2025
what: On 27 April Boeing reported a first-quarter loss with charges on fixed-price defence programmes and the war in Ukraine, negative operating cash flow of 3.2 billion dollars, and said the first 777-9 delivery is now expected in 2025.
why: Explains the -22% month together with a falling market (-9%).

title: Emirates orders 90 more 777Xs in Dubai
what: On 13 November, at the Dubai Airshow, Emirates ordered 90 more Boeing 777Xs, 55 of the 777-9 and 35 of the 777-8, bringing its total 777X order to 205. Stock markets rallied strongly in November; the S&P 500 gained 9%.
why: Explains the +24% month: big orders plus the market. Boeing ended 2023 up 37%, just before the door-plug accident.

title: A door plug blows out of a new 737 MAX 9
what: On 5 January a door plug blew out of an Alaska Airlines 737 MAX 9 shortly after take-off from Portland; all 177 people on board survived. The FAA grounded similar planes, and inspections found loose parts on others. Chief executive Dave Calhoun admitted a 'quality escape', and the FAA opened an investigation into Boeing's production.
why: Explains the -19% month: the end of Boeing's recovery story and the start of a second safety crisis.

title: Boeing buys back Spirit and picks Kelly Ortberg
what: On 1 July Boeing agreed to buy Spirit AeroSystems, the Wichita supplier that builds 737 fuselages and was spun off from Boeing in 2005, in an all-stock deal worth about 4.7 billion dollars. On 31 July it named Kelly Ortberg, a former head of Rockwell Collins, as chief executive from 8 August. Dave Calhoun, who announced in March that he would step down after the door-plug accident, leaves on 7 August.
why: The repair programme begins: bring quality back in-house and bring in an engineer as boss.

title: 33,000 machinists strike
what: On 13 September more than 33,000 Boeing machinists, mostly around Seattle, went on strike after 94.6% rejected a contract with a 25% raise over four years. Production of the 737, 767 and 777 has stopped.
why: Explains the -12% month; the strike cost Boeing an estimated 5 billion dollars by early October and ended on 4 November with a 38% raise.

title: Boeing raises 21 billion dollars of new capital
what: On 28 October Boeing sold 112.5 million new shares at 143 dollars and 5 billion dollars of mandatory convertible preferred shares, raising about 21 billion dollars to protect its credit rating. The machinists' strike is still on.
why: The dilution price of five years of crises; the stock bottomed around here.

title: Boeing wins the next-generation fighter
what: On 21 March the US Air Force awarded Boeing the contract to build its next-generation air dominance fighter, a programme worth more than 20 billion dollars.
why: A much-needed win for the defence side, which had suffered heavy losses on fixed-price programmes.

title: Regulators clear the Spirit deal
what: The US Federal Trade Commission asked Boeing to sell Spirit AeroSystems businesses that supply Airbus and Malaysia's Subang to clear the takeover, and EU regulators said the remedy addressed their concerns. Airbus is taking over Spirit's Airbus work.
why: Boeing owns its fuselage supplier again; the month was +15%.

title: China to buy 200 Boeing jets
what: On 20 May China confirmed it will buy 200 Boeing aircraft after a summit between the Chinese and US presidents.
why: Political orders as a support for the recovery; the share price, however, was below its 2019 peak by more than half.
